title: Tamarind chutney
subtitle: Sweet and sour tamarind dipping sauce
excerpt: A thick, date-sweetened tamarind sauce with cumin and ginger. The essential condiment for Indian street food: chaat, samosas, bhajis, and dahi puri. Made in 15 minutes and keeps in the fridge for weeks.
sourceNotes: Tamarind chutney (imli ki chutney) is a foundational Indian condiment found throughout the subcontinent, essential to chaat cooking. Cross-referenced with Madhur Jaffrey, Indian Cooking (1982) and Monica Bhide for spice ratios.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes in an ice cube tray for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the recipe and keep in the fridge for up to 4 weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Improves with 24 hours in the fridge. Serve at room temperature.

content.text: Tamarind chutney is the dark, sweet-sour sauce spooned over samosas, drizzled on dahi puri, and eaten with everything fried on an Indian street food stall. It is simple and very fast to make. You need tamarind paste (concentrated, sold in jars) or tamarind block (which must be soaked and strained). Dates provide the sweetness; cumin, ginger, and chilli the spice.

items.prepNote: concentrated tamarind paste from a jar; or 80 g tamarind block dissolved in 150 ml hot water and strained
pitted; or 4 tbsp soft brown sugar

content.text: Blend the dates with 100 ml of the water until smooth.
Combine the tamarind paste, date purée, and remaining 100 ml water in a small saucepan. Add the cumin, ginger, chilli flakes, and salt. Stir well.
Simmer over medium heat for 5 to 8 minutes, stirring, until the sauce thickens to a coating consistency. It will thicken further on cooling.
Taste and adjust: more tamarind for sourness, more dates or sugar for sweetness, more salt. Cool completely before storing in a jar in the fridge.

items.cause: Too much tamarind or insufficient sweetener
items.fix: Add more date purée or a teaspoon of sugar and simmer for 2 more minutes.
Thin with a tablespoon of warm water at a time, stirring well.
Toast cumin seeds in a dry pan for 1 minute, then grind. This makes a significant difference to the flavour.

items.symptom: The dates did not blend smoothly
items.cause: Too dry or not enough water
items.fix: Soak the dates in hot water for 10 minutes before blending. Add more water if needed.

content.text: Tamarind chutney is one of the two canonical chutneys of Indian chaat cooking (the other is hari chutney, a green coriander and mint sauce). The pair appear together on almost every chaat plate across India: the green sauce for freshness, the tamarind sauce for depth and sweetness. The tamarind itself is the fruit of the tamarind tree, pressed and concentrated; it provides acidity without the astringency of citrus. The chutney keeps well in the fridge and is useful to have on hand for any Indian-style snack or street food dish.
